q: Kestrel IT operations hands over a firewall CSV (E-04) with no hash or manifest. The lab computes its SHA-256 at intake at 16:40 IST. What can the lab later say on the strength of that value alone?
options: The CSV is the complete and unaltered output of the firewall for 11 to 12 March
The CSV has not changed since export, because CSV files cannot be edited without trace
The file has not changed since intake; its earlier history must come from the exporter
Nothing useful, because a hash only has value when it is computed by the data's provider
explanation: A hash taken at intake anchors the item's state from intake onwards. Completeness and pre-intake history depend on IT operations, who exported it. The 'complete and unaltered output' option claims far more than the lab observed.

q: The SHA-256 of the received mailbox archive (E-03) matches the value on the provider's export manifest. Which statement is best supported?
options: The lab holds the file the provider says it exported; the export filter may still have missed relevant mail
The pricing-team mailbox held no other relevant messages for the period, because the provider's export is a full copy of the mailbox
The provider's mail platform is shown to have been free of tampering throughout March 2026
The match proves that every message in the archive was sent by the account holder
explanation: The match ties the lab copy to the provider's export. It says nothing about what the export's filter left out, about the platform's integrity, or about who wrote the messages.

q: In section 5 of the course transcript, one byte of working.dd is changed at offset 100000, yet the comparison reports 'differ: char 100001'. Why?
options: The change also moved the next byte, so the comparison reports the second altered position
The comparison skips the first byte of every file because it holds a header
SHA-256 works on blocks, so the reported position is rounded up to the next unit
Offsets count from zero, while the comparison numbers bytes starting at one
explanation: Offset 100000 is the 100,001st byte when counting from one, which is how the byte comparison reports positions. Hashing plays no part in the reported position.

q: In the transcript, sections 2 and 3 both show e3a74e55…0f21 for evidence.dd. What does section 3 add that section 2 does not?
options: It proves the source suspect.dev was not modified before section 1 was run
It re-reads the stored file, showing what is at rest matches what was read
It converts the stream digest into a format a court will accept as an image hash
Nothing; section 3 repeats section 2 so that a second examiner can sign it
explanation: Section 2 hashes the stream as it was written; section 3 hashes the file as stored, confirming the write. Neither can speak to the source's state before section 1.

q: Section 6 of the transcript records an MD5 value for evidence.dd. How should that value be treated in the case record?
options: As the primary value, since a shorter digest is quicker for others to compare
As a secondary value kept for older records; SHA-256 stays the primary integrity value
As proof that the image is genuine, because two different algorithms now agree with each other
As redundant, so it should be deleted from the record to avoid confusing the reader
explanation: The transcript labels MD5 'legacy compatibility only'. MD5 has known practical collisions, so it supports compatibility, not primary integrity. Two digests agreeing still only show bit-identity.

q: The Kestrel question is whether the spreadsheet left the company network. The analyst's plan covers only files on laptop E-01. Using source-based classification, what is the most significant gap?
options: Embedded document properties inside the spreadsheet have not yet been listed
The laptop's own operating-system logs have not been scheduled for parsing
The printed copy E-05 has not been compared line by line with the digital spreadsheet
Network-side records held elsewhere, such as firewall, proxy or mail platform logs
explanation: SP 800-86's sources include network traffic and applications, which are often held off the endpoint. Records of data leaving the network are most likely there, not in the laptop's files.

q: Laptop E-01 arrived powered off. A draft report later states which programs were running when the leak occurred. What is the problem?
options: No memory or running state from before shutdown was available, so that claim needs other support
Running programs must always be inferred from the disk image, which has not been made yet
The claim is acceptable provided the laptop is switched on again in the lab so the examiner can confirm which programs start up
The receipt should have listed the running programs at intake for the claim to stand
explanation: Volatile state is lost at power-off, and the receipt recorded that state. Switching the laptop on would change evidence and would not show what ran earlier.

q: An HR manager forwards a screenshot of a chat message apparently sent by the employee. How should the lab classify and handle it?
options: As the original record, since it shows the message exactly as the employee saw it
As system-generated evidence, so it can be relied on without further corroboration
As a derived presentation kept as a received item; seek the native record within scope
As inadmissible material that should be returned to HR without being logged
explanation: A screenshot is a rendering of a record, without its metadata. It is kept and logged as received, and the native message is requested through the authorised route. Discarding it loses a received item.

q: The pricing spreadsheet's 'author' property names the suspected employee. What is the soundest reading?
options: It identifies who typed the figures, because the field is written by the operating system
It is unreliable and should be excluded, because document properties are user-editable
It proves the file was last saved on laptop E-01, since the name matches its user
It is application metadata from a configured name; treat it as a lead to corroborate
explanation: The application writes the author field from a configured user name, which can be inherited or edited. It is a hybrid record: neither an identification nor something to discard.

q: An analyst produces a timeline CSV by parsing a working copy of the laptop image. What must the record of that CSV include for it to be checkable?
options: The source item and its hash, plus the tool, version and settings used
A screenshot of the tool's display at the moment the CSV was produced
A fresh SHA-256 of the CSV only, since the CSV is now the evidence item
The analyst's signature and the date, which together establish the CSV's provenance
explanation: A derived artefact is trustworthy through its verified source and recorded process, which let a second examiner re-create it. Hashing the CSV alone fixes the output but not how it was made.

q: To limit personal data, the team considers a targeted collection of named folders instead of a full image of E-01. What is the main trade-off?
options: Targeted collection cannot be hashed, so integrity can no longer be demonstrated
There is none, provided the folder list was agreed with the authorising party
Less data and intrusion, but no later answers about content it never captured
A full image avoids all privacy obligations, since it is only kept within the lab
explanation: Targeted collections reduce volume and intrusion but cannot answer questions about data they did not capture, such as deleted content. Both approaches can be hashed and both carry privacy duties.

q: The receipt describes E-02 as 'marked 32 GB' rather than '32 GB drive'. Why is that wording preferred?
options: Capacities above 16 GB must be measured before any receipt can be signed
The marking is an observed label; the capacity the device reports is set at acquisition
Flash drives always hold less than their label states, so writing '32 GB drive' would put a false statement on the receipt
It allows the lab to replace the drive later with one of the same marking
explanation: A receipt records observations. The reported capacity is established when the drive is acquired and may differ from the label. The other options invent rules or misstate the reason.

q: Messages in E-03 suggest the employee also used a personal phone, which the receipt records as outside scope. What should the examiner do?
options: Record the observation and refer the scope question to the authorising party
Ask the employee to hand over the phone, since the messages make it relevant
Ignore the phone entirely and leave the observation out of the notes
Request the phone's backups from the employee's personal cloud account directly
explanation: Extending collection is a scope decision for the authorising party. The examiner records what was seen and does not improvise collection, nor hide the observation.

q: Firewall CSV E-04 has timestamps with no time-zone marker, and the receipt is written in IST. What should happen before correlating the two?
options: Assume IST, because the firewall is physically located in the Pune office
Subtract five and a half hours, because network devices always log in UTC
Correlate by order of events only, since absolute times are not needed
Confirm the export's time basis and the device clock with the exporter
explanation: The time basis of a provider export must be established from the source, not assumed. Either assumption could misplace events by 5 h 30 min; ordering alone fails across systems.

q: A USB connection record on the laptop was central in the Kestrel case. In a different case, the same type of record is ignored. Which concept explains this?
options: Records of this type are only valid when the USB drive itself is also seized
System-generated records lose evidential weight after a fixed retention period
An artefact becomes evidence only when it is relevant to a question in the case
Only artefacts found in unallocated space are treated as evidence in practice
explanation: An artefact is a trace; it becomes evidence relative to the case's questions. The other options invent rules about validity or weight.

q: Why does the lab keep printout E-05 in its own sealed envelope instead of scanning it and discarding the paper?
options: A scan would carry the original spreadsheet's file metadata, which would duplicate E-03
It is a physical item that may matter to other examinations, and no scan replaces it
Paper documents are the strongest evidence type and outrank any digital record
Scanning would change its hash, so the printout could no longer be verified
explanation: The printout is physical evidence in its own right and may be needed by other disciplines. It carries none of the file's metadata, and paper has no hash; its anchor is the envelope and intake note.

q: The provider re-zips the same mailbox messages and the new archive's SHA-256 differs from E-03's manifest value. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The messages must have been altered, because identical content always gives the same archive hash
SHA-256 is unreliable for archives, so MD5 should be used for compressed files instead
The lab's copy of E-03 has been corrupted and should be replaced with the new archive
The hash covers the container's bytes, which can change on re-packing; record which object was hashed
explanation: An archive hash covers the container, whose bytes depend on packing details such as stored times and compression. The contents may be unchanged; compare at the level that was hashed.

q: A colleague says the matching SHA-256 values prove evidence.dd is authentic. What is the most accurate correction?
options: A match shows bit-identity with what was hashed earlier, not that the source was the right one or unaltered before
A match proves authenticity only if the MD5 value in section 6 also matches, since two algorithms together rule out every alteration
A match is meaningless unless the hash was computed on the original hardware
A match proves authenticity, but only for images smaller than 16 MiB
explanation: A digest match is strong evidence that two sets of bits are identical. It cannot show that the right source was chosen or that the source was unaltered before section 1.

q: A vendor points to a NIST CFTT report on its imaging tool. How should the lab treat that report?
options: As certification that any version of the tool may be used without further checks
As irrelevant, because CFTT only tests tools used by government agencies
As a record of how a tested version behaved; the lab still checks its own version and setup
As a legal guarantee that images made with the tool will be admitted in Indian courts
explanation: CFTT reports describe how a particular tool version behaved under test. They are not certifications or legal guarantees, and they do not replace the lab's checks of its own configuration.

q: Which pair of Kestrel items, if they agree, gives the strongest corroboration that the spreadsheet was copied to removable media?
options: Two transfer copies of the firewall CSV that have identical SHA-256 values
A USB attachment record on the laptop and the spreadsheet found on drive E-02
The forensic copy and the working copy of the laptop image matching each other
The mailbox archive hash and the value printed on the export manifest
explanation: The host record and the drive's contents are independent sources recording related facts. The other pairs are copies of one source agreeing with each other, which confirms copying only.

q: The team decides that the perimeter firewall's own log store can wait until next month, because logs are non-volatile. What is the main risk in that plan?
options: None, because non-volatile records survive power loss and remain available indefinitely
The firewall export E-04 already contains every record, so later requests add nothing
Requesting firewall logs is outside any internal investigation's authorised scope
Rotation or retention limits may delete the records first; ask the holder to preserve them early
explanation: Persistent does not mean permanent: logs rotate and retention settings delete old records. Preservation should be requested early within scope. E-04 is a filtered export, not the whole store.

q: File-system timestamps on the spreadsheet in E-02 disagree with the modification date in its embedded document properties. What is the best first response?
options: Treat both as facts written by different layers, and explain the difference
Prefer the file-system timestamps, since the operating system cannot be wrong
Prefer the embedded properties, since they travel with the file between systems
Discard both, because conflicting metadata shows the file has been tampered with
explanation: Embedded and file-system metadata are written at different moments by different layers, and copying or editing commonly makes them diverge. The disagreement is data to explain.

q: The mailbox export E-03 covers 1 to 12 March. The investigation now needs to know whether pricing files were emailed in February. What follows?
options: E-03 already shows nothing was emailed in February, because no February messages appear anywhere in the archive
The lab may log in to the mail platform to search February itself
E-03 cannot answer it; request a new export, if February is within the authorised scope
February can be inferred from March traffic patterns in the firewall CSV
explanation: An export answers only what its filter allowed. Absence from a March export says nothing about February, and the lab does not access provider systems outside the authorised route.

q: Which control most directly lets the lab detect an accidental write to a working copy of the laptop image, as illustrated in section 5 of the transcript?
options: Keeping the working copy on an encrypted volume that only the case analyst can open
Re-hashing the working copy after tool use and comparing it with the forensic copy's value
Renaming the working copy with the case number so it cannot be confused with other files
Storing an MD5 value as well, because MD5 is more sensitive to single-byte changes
explanation: Re-verification against the anchor exposes any change, as the one-byte edit in section 5 shows. Encryption and naming control access and confusion, not detection; MD5 is no more sensitive.

q: How does this lesson use the SWGDE Best Practices for Computer Forensic Acquisition?
options: As a step-by-step procedure that every acquisition in this course must follow word for word
As a legal standard whose use guarantees the admissibility of any resulting image
As a list of tested tools that the course recommends for laptop acquisition
As guidance for the general point that acquisition is planned, documented and verified
explanation: The lesson relies on SWGDE only for that general point and directs learners to the current version for specifics. Best-practice guidance is not a legal guarantee or a tool list.
